messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Civil Servant
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miriam Holloway is a 51-year-old married European American woman who has worked for nearly two decades as a civil servant in a mid-sized municipal office, processing permits and coordinating with contractors and inspectors. She presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a toxic chemical exposure incident that she describes, haltingly, as the worst thing that has ever happened to her — though she struggles to say much more than that without losing her way.

The incident occurred on a routine site visit Miriam was required to attend as part of her regulatory oversight duties. She had accompanied a colleague to inspect a storage facility where, without warning, a pressurised container ruptured. The release was sudden and violent — a hissing roar that filled the space before anyone understood what was happening, followed by a burning sensation in her throat and eyes, and voices around her dissolving into a blur of shouting she could not parse. Workers were yelling in a mixture of languages, none of it coalescing into meaning. She remembers the smell most of all — sharp, chemical, wrong — and the sensation of being grabbed by the arm and pulled toward the exit by someone she could not identify. Emergency services arrived. There were paramedics, a stretcher, the interior of an ambulance. She was hospitalised for two days and discharged with no lasting physiological damage, though the discharge felt less like relief than abandonment.

In the weeks that followed, Miriam found herself unable to reconstruct what had happened in any coherent sequence. When her husband gently asked what the facility had looked like, or what she had been doing in the moments before the rupture, she would begin and then stop — the thread simply gone, as though the memory existed somewhere she could not reach deliberately. She told her GP that she could not explain it properly, and partway through the attempt she had gone quiet and asked to talk about something else. What frightened her most was not the forgetting itself but the sense that the event was somehow still inside her, undigested, shapeless — present as sensation rather than story.

By autumn she had reorganised her daily life around a small number of places she trusted: her home, her immediate office, and a single route between them. Unpredictable situations had become intolerable. When a meeting ran over and she was asked to cover a colleague's desk in a different part of the building, she experienced a wave of alarm so acute that she left early and said she felt unwell. She had come to believe that safety was a property of specific, known spaces — not a general condition of the world. Loud or unexpected sounds in the office — a door slamming, a phone ringing from an unfamiliar extension — brought her instantly to a state of vigilance that took long minutes to subside. Strangers approaching her desk without prior context, delivery personnel, unfamiliar contractors, had become genuinely threatening in a way she found difficult to justify but impossible to dismiss.

At work, where her role requires her to coordinate daily with contractors and inspectors — often people she does not know — Miriam had taken to rehearsing every exchange in advance, scripting her own lines as though the conversation were a document to be filed. She had stopped attending the monthly all-staff briefings, citing scheduling conflicts. She refused all physical contact, including the handshakes that are ordinary currency in her professional world, and had declined two medical appointments — one a routine physical examination — because the prospect of a clinical environment, the smell of it, the equipment, had become something she could not bring herself to approach. Her husband had noticed that she flinched when he touched her shoulder, and had stopped trying.

What finally brought Miriam to seek help was a performance review in which her supervisor noted, kindly but clearly, that her engagement with external stakeholders had declined markedly and that colleagues had raised concerns. She sat in the car afterwards and wept for a long time. She is most afraid, she said at intake, that she will never be able to explain what happened — not to her husband, not to a therapist, not even to herself. What she is hoping for, she added quietly, is simply to be able to walk into a room without knowing exactly what will happen next and still feel that she will be all right.
